introduction-hitting-the-wall.core: Single-GPU training hits two walls: it's too slow (the data or compute is too big, which data parallelism fixes) or the model is too big (it doesn't fit in memory, which model parallelism, ZeRO and 3D parallelism fix).

first_principles.problem: A model takes three months to train on one GPU, or simply won't fit in its memory.
truths: Work can be split across devices.

analogy.title: Filling a swimming pool with a garden hose
analogy.story: Use more hoses (data parallel), or split the pool into sections (model parallel).
analogy.breaks: Parallelism has overheads, and scaling efficiency drops as communication grows.

example.title: Choosing a strategy
flow: ResNet on ImageNet, slow → DDP on 8 GPUs
70B LLM doesn't fit → TP + PP + ZeRO across 64 GPUs

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The strategy matches the wall you've hit.

example.outcome: you can diagnose which parallelism you need.

check.q: Which parallelism addresses a model that doesn't fit on one GPU?
check.a: Model parallelism (tensor or pipeline), often combined with ZeRO/FSDP.

data-parallelism-ddp-the-cloning-techniq.core: Distributed Data Parallel puts a full copy of the model on each GPU, splits each batch across them, computes gradients independently, then all-reduces the gradients so every replica applies the same update. Throughput scales with the number of GPUs.

first_principles.problem: Training on one GPU is too slow, but the model fits on a single GPU.
truths: Gradients from different data can be averaged.
Identical replicas stay in sync with identical updates.
Communication overhead grows with model size.
derivation: Scale **batch size and learning rate** appropriately.

analogy.title: Cloning a student to study faster
analogy.story: Each clone reads a different chapter, then they share notes so everyone learns everything.
analogy.breaks: Each GPU must hold the whole model, optimizer and gradients, so it doesn't help models that are too big.

example.title: Launching DDP

code.text:
torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 train.py
# in train.py: model = DDP(model.to(local_rank), device_ids=[local_rank])
#              sampler = DistributedSampler(dataset)

example.outcome: faster training for models that fit.

check.q: What's synchronised between replicas in DDP?
check.a: Gradients, via all-reduce, so every replica applies the same weight update.

model-parallelism-tensor-parallelism-tp.core: Tensor parallelism splits individual layers' weight matrices across GPUs (column- and row-wise, as in Megatron-LM). Each GPU computes part of every matrix multiply, then results are combined with all-reduce or all-gather inside the layer, so huge layers fit.

first_principles.problem: A single layer's weights or activations exceed one GPU's memory.

analogy.title: Several chefs each chopping part of one huge vegetable
analogy.story: Each handles a section, then they combine the pieces for the next step.
analogy.breaks: Heavy communication per layer makes cross-node TP slow.

example.title: TP of an MLP block
flow: W1 split by columns: GPU0, GPU1

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each GPU holds half the weights.

example.outcome: layers too big for one GPU become trainable.

check.q: Why is tensor parallelism usually confined to GPUs within one node?
check.a: It requires communication within every layer, which needs very high-bandwidth intra-node links like NVLink.

model-parallelism-pipeline-parallelism-p.core: Pipeline parallelism splits the model by layers into stages on different GPUs, like an assembly line. Micro-batches flow through the stages (GPipe, 1F1B schedules) to reduce idle 'bubbles' while each stage works on a different micro-batch.

first_principles.problem: A model with many layers doesn't fit, and tensor parallelism across nodes is too communication-heavy.
truths: Layers can be assigned to different devices.
derivation: **Schedule** forward and backward passes (1F1B) to minimise bubbles.

analogy.title: A car assembly line
analogy.story: Each station adds parts and passes the car on; several cars are in progress at once.
analogy.breaks: Unbalanced stages and bubbles reduce efficiency, and large micro-batch counts increase activation memory.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Fits across nodes with modest communication.

check.a: Idle time on pipeline stages while waiting for micro-batches to arrive from earlier stages or for backward passes.

zero-zero-redundancy-optimizer-the-memor.core: In plain DDP every GPU stores a full copy of the optimizer states, gradients and parameters, which is redundant. ZeRO (DeepSpeed) and FSDP shard them across GPUs: stage 1 shards optimizer states, stage 2 adds gradients, stage 3 adds parameters, gathering pieces just in time.

first_principles.problem: Adam's optimizer states alone are about 12 bytes per parameter, so a 10B model's training state can't fit even when the weights do.
truths: Each GPU only needs its shard most of the time.
Gathering on demand trades communication for memory.

analogy.title: A study group splitting the notes
analogy.story: Instead of everyone keeping a full copy of every textbook, each person keeps a section and shares it when needed.
analogy.breaks: Stage 3 adds communication, and performance depends on interconnect speed.

example.title: Memory per GPU for a 7B model on 8 GPUs

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The model trains on commodity 40–80 GB GPUs.

check.q: What does ZeRO stage 3 (or FSDP full sharding) shard?
check.a: Optimizer states, gradients and model parameters across all data-parallel GPUs.

combining-strategies-3d-parallelism.core: The largest models combine tensor parallelism (within a node, over NVLink), pipeline parallelism (across nodes, by layers) and data parallelism (replicating the whole pipeline, often with ZeRO), mapping each to the network tier it suits best.

first_principles.problem: No single strategy can train a 175B+ model efficiently on thousands of GPUs.
truths: Each strategy has different communication needs.
The hardware has tiers of bandwidth.
Mapping strategy to tier maximises efficiency.

analogy.title: A large construction project
analogy.story: Teams of specialists work closely on a floor (TP), floors are built in sequence (PP), and identical buildings go up in parallel (DP).
analogy.breaks: Configuration is complex, and frameworks (Megatron, DeepSpeed, NeMo) help.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each communication pattern uses the right links.

check.q: In 3D parallelism, how is the total GPU count determined?
check.a: As the product of tensor-parallel, pipeline-parallel and data-parallel degrees (TP × PP × DP).
